body:
# the contributor audit of fixed-sector Lorentz maxima

Source: `candidate 1a5bfc0fdb9108c3`.


not an audit of a global Lorentz inequality or of OC; neither is claimed.

The fixed six positive sector areas give positive lower radius bounds from
the PSD diagonal and finite upper bounds from neighboring core products.
Thus the feasible set is closed in a compact positive box. Every chord,
cap area, and denominator in the objective is strictly positive, so the
row objective is continuous and attains its maximum. Actual realization
uses the independently proved exact-sector PSD equivalence, rather than
an assumed realization of arbitrary radius data.

I checked both projective-coordinate formulas. For a selected coordinate
the quadratic coefficient is strictly positive. For a nonselected one,
zero quadratic coefficient leaves a strictly negative linear derivative;
therefore a stationary one-coordinate variation always has positive
second variation. Only convexity in the fractional coordinate tau is
used. The sign of its derivative agrees with the inverse-chord derivative.

Increasing one endpoint radius up to its two adjacent core bounds raises
every changed matrix entry while preserving nonpositive off-diagonals.
The comparison of quadratic forms on absolute vectors proves PSD
preservation, including the closed limiting bound. Homogeneity then
forces a positive chord derivative unless all three vanish. Both endpoints
of a positive-derivative chord must be core-adjacent. If all derivatives
vanish, all six endpoints must be core-adjacent. This proves respectively
at least two and at least three core sectors. The direct derivative
formulas with H=2Phi_i-f_i follow by differentiating z_j=q_j x_j/M and
agree with these signs, including the stationary case.

Positive definiteness is incompatible with a local maximum: decreasing
any single radius preserves it for sufficiently small change and improves
the adjacent core inequalities. A negative chord derivative supplies a
first-order increase; if all vanish, the strict fractional-coordinate
curvature supplies an increase. No open-core assumption is needed here.

For exactly two cores, I checked all four enumerated edge pairs after
placing a positive-derivative chord at nodes 1 and 4. They are exactly
(0,3), (0,4), (1,3), and (1,4). Deleting those two edges produces the
blocks stated in the source. At a core-preserving transfer, the shrinking
radius lies in the hypothesized positive-definite block, which remains
positive definite locally. The growing radius lies in the other block,
whose entries increase and whose internal edges retain strict negative
sign for small change. The shared edge remains zero. Thus these are
genuinely feasible variations. The two short/long patterns force both
other derivatives positive if the short block is positive definite, or
both zero if the long block is positive definite. The two length-three
patterns force one other derivative zero and the last negative, then
admit a strictly improving boundary transfer. Each contradicts weighted
homogeneity. This exhausts the possible two-core patterns.

Both blocks are therefore singular irreducible PSD Z-matrices. Their
least Rayleigh vectors can be chosen nonnegative; the zero-coordinate
equation propagates zeros along the path, proving strict positivity.
The exact reconstruction's Gram identity forces all node slacks to
vanish and fixes every positive edge charge by the null-vector ratio.
Blockwise scaling has no effect on those ratios. There are four and only
four positive-excess sectors, each contributing a strict vertex, while
all original ray endpoints are on edge interiors. The resulting polygon
is the unique quadrilateral. Retaining actual endpoint supports then
places any original realizing convex body inside that quadrilateral;
equal positive areas force equality. This last step treats curved bodies
and does not merely prove uniqueness of one polygonal replacement.

The reduction preserves each of the six sectors and hence each selected
cap/profile budget. It does not preserve neighboring mixed fibers.
Three-or-more-core strata and the global row inequality on quadrilaterals
remain explicit missing obligations.

## Appended Sections 8--11: independent root audit

These sections also PASS. At a PD path block with at least three nodes,
an internal radius has two strict excess neighbors and can move both
ways. The previously checked projective curvature excludes a local
maximum even when the first derivative vanishes. Thus every large block
is singular. Positive least eigenvectors in each block reconstruct node
slack equal to the corresponding least eigenvalue; the actual polygon
has exactly p+v_PD strict vertices. All cycle edge partitions with p<=3
give the initial seven-vertex bound.

The six-vertex refinement correctly varies the entire PD principal
complement, rather than incorrectly insisting that old zero edges
between PD blocks remain zero. A radius two or more nodes away from a
sole singular singleton can decrease without changing its singular row
or column. The three such consecutive endpoints touch all three chords,
forcing every chord derivative positive, a contradiction. For a sole
singular two-node block, the two interior PD-complement endpoints force
two derivatives positive. The remaining one is negative, and the stated
core-preserving transfer shrinks its PD endpoint while growing the
adjacent singular endpoint. Both separating zero edges remain unchanged;
the PD complement tolerates its internal changes by openness, and the
singular block's entrywise increase preserves PSD. This is a strict gain.

Two adjacent singular singletons would put four consecutive nonzero
ray endpoints on one line, including opposite rays, which is impossible.
Enumerating the remaining positive-edge graphs leaves exactly the two
six-vertex patterns listed as A and B. This proves the finite six-vertex
reduction; no row inequality is inferred merely from that reduction.

For type B, the two singleton equations yield A=Br/(B+r) and
a=bt/(b+t). I independently expanded the two remaining determinants;
their coefficients are linear in 1/(2X),1/(2Y) and give exactly the two
conditional upper bounds in Section 10. The core lower bounds supply
the nonpositive off-diagonal signs, and positive diagonals make these
determinants necessary and sufficient for each block. The exact-sector
theorem therefore proves actual realization, including limiting equalities.

The rational six vertices in Section 11 have the claimed ray intersections
and sector areas. With B=t=1, b=r=11/10 their two blocks have equal
diagonals, so the equal-coefficient inserted vertices agree with the
positive least-eigenvector construction. I checked k=117/50,
q_1=q_3=29/25, q_2=2423/2100 and the sorted excess 277/1050.
Thus the half-cap exclusion is indeed false; this example neither meets
the smaller ceiling 128/279 nor contradicts the separate root theorem
`candidate 10ff75afdda8a25f`.

## Sections 12--13: at least two singular blocks and the pentagon reduction

increase and forces its chord derivative strictly negative. The opposite
radius lies away from the singular path in the full PD complement and
can decrease, forcing that same derivative strictly positive. Equality
is excluded in both cases by the established projective curvature.

For a unique singular four-node path, its two internal radii force two
negative chord derivatives. Homogeneity makes the remaining derivative
positive. The simultaneous growth of both singular boundary radii and
shrinkage of both complementary PD radii preserves the separating core
products. Changes within the singular block are entrywise increases
with strict negative internal edges retained; the entire PD complement
tolerates the new internal off-diagonal term by openness. The displayed
first variation is strictly positive. Together with the preceding
one/two-node exclusions and the exactly-two-core theorem, this proves
at least two singular blocks at every row maximum.

I rechecked the resulting cycle-graph enumeration. The only remaining
six-vertex case is type B, excluded under q_i/k<=128/279 by the root
8/17 theorem. The four listed five-vertex block patterns are exactly
the possibilities from the vertex formula p+v_PD and the nonadjacent
singular-singleton restriction. Thus the cap-band reduction to an actual
polygon with at most five vertices is proved; its separate row inequality
is still required.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
